takeaway: ShiftLock queues contending RDMA writers and hands locks directly between clients, replacing server-bound retries with reliable notifications while preserving fast reader-writer acquisition and failure recovery.
background: One-sided RDMA locks mutate entries in a server's memory without its CPU, often acquiring an uncontended lock in one network round trip. Reader-writer locks permit shared reads, and MCS queue locks hand ownership directly to a successor on one machine.
villain: Under skew and concurrency, failed one-sided atomics repeatedly hit the same lock-server RNIC, consuming inbound IOPS and increasing queueing latency; tuning backoff only reduces retries. A distributed MCS translation would need scalable client connectivity, compact routing, reader semantics, fairness, and recovery from broken queues.
approach: ShiftLock uses masked 128-bit RDMA atomics for a compact queue-tail/reader/release/epoch entry and dynamic-connected two-sided Sends for successor and handover notices. Writers form an MCS queue, readers count concurrently, epochs alternate ownership after bounded writer batches, and server-mediated lease recovery prevents stale ABA resets.
impact: The design retains one-roundtrip uncontended acquisition but moves contended coordination off the central RNIC. It shows that judicious two-sided client communication can improve an otherwise one-sided RDMA abstraction without dedicating polling CPUs.

evaluation.overview: Uniform and Zipfian microbenchmarks vary read mix, locks, clients, and skew; transaction traces, a Redis banking application, latency/verb decomposition, fairness tuning, and injected client failures test broader behavior.
evaluation.implemented: A 7.2-KLOC Rust implementation using Mellanox dynamic connection, 16-byte lock entries, extended CAS/FAA, buffered Send/Recv notifications, reader/writer epochs, a 16-writer fairness threshold, and 10-ms lease plus server-era recovery.
evaluation.setting: Six dual-socket 48-core machines with 128 GB DRAM and ConnectX-5 100-Gbps RNICs; one is the lock server and five run 240 total clients. Default tests use ten million locks on Ubuntu 18.04/Linux 4.15.

results.text: Under skewed high-contention microbenchmarks, ShiftLock reports up to 3.62× the goodput and up to 76.6% lower 99th-percentile latency than evaluated RDMA-lock alternatives.
ShiftLock improves TATP goodput by 1.25×–2.85× and TPC-C goodput by 1.09×–2.14× over other RDMA locks while providing comparable or lower transaction latency.
In the Redis-backed banking application, ShiftLock reaches 36.55 K transactions/s versus RedLock's 5.56 K and reduces median and 99th-percentile latency by 62.9% and 95.2%.

limitations: ShiftLock requires modern RNIC support for dynamic connection and masked 128-bit extended atomics. Its centralized server RNIC remains the eventual throughput bottleneck. Lease recovery assumes bounded clock-rate drift, waits three lease periods, invokes server CPUs, and under tested failures trails DSLR. Evaluation uses six machines, synthetic critical sections/failures, and a Redis comparison whose RedLock traffic uses IP over InfiniBand.
phd_group_signal: The paper reintroduces a local queue-lock principle under RDMA constraints and carefully engineers routing, message progress, bit layout, fairness, and recovery. It exemplifies network/storage concurrency research backed by proofs, hardware counters, applications, and failure tests.

claims.text: A writer atomically replaces the queue tail, notifies its predecessor through a dynamically connected RDMA Send, waits locally, and later receives ownership directly rather than retrying the server entry.
A one-bit epoch releases the current waiting-reader cohort after at most 16 consecutive writers, while a non-null writer tail blocks newly arriving readers, preventing starvation in both directions.
